title: Mindfulness of breathing
hook: of all the things to watch, why the breath? one answer from the suttas, and one from a neighbor
tomorrow: what is the peace the whole path is pointing at?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sack of grains: the body known, part by part, no verdict. Today, the one part of the body that moves all by itself.
screen: `THE BODY KNOWN.` → `THE PART THAT MOVES ITSELF.`

segments.voice: A coach before a free throw, a nurse before a shot, a friend before a hard phone call: take a breath. So, of all the things a person could watch, why the breath? It's always here, wherever you are. It runs on its own, and it also lets you steer. And it never repeats: this breath isn't the last one. That makes it a teacher you carry everywhere.
screen: `TAKE A BREATH.` → `ALWAYS HERE. NEVER THE SAME.` → `WHY THE BREATH?`

segments.voice: In the Anapanasati Sutta, anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing, begins very small. Breathing in long, know: I breathe in long. Breathing in short, know: short. Then sense the whole body breathing. Then let the body calm. That's four steps; the sutta lays out sixteen, in four sets of four, moving from the body to feelings, to the mind, to letting go. In another sutta the Buddha compares the practice to a rain that comes out of season at the end of the hot months, settling the dust all at once. Now, a neighbor. In Genesis, a book Jews and Christians share, the breath arrives as a gift. In the King James words: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Shared ground: both traditions point at the breath as the closest sign of being alive, and both slow down for it. One honest difference: in Genesis the breath comes from God, and noticing it can turn a person toward the giver. The Buddha's practice doesn't ask where the breath came from. It watches it come, and go, and come again.
screen: `LONG IS LONG. SHORT IS SHORT.` · `SIXTEEN STEPS, FOUR BY FOUR.` · `THE BREATH OF LIFE, IN GENESIS.` · `GIVEN, OR JUST WATCHED.` · then, large: `THE BREATH AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes or lower them, and breathe without steering. When a breath is long, know it's long; when it's short, know it's short. Those are the first two steps of sixteen, and two minutes is a fine place to start.
Mindfulness of breathing: knowing each breath as it is, in and out. In Pali, anapanasati. Sixteen steps, and the first is simply knowing.
Hold on to this: the breath again, whenever you lose your place. Twenty-seven of forty.

howItsDone: Mindfulness of breathing is taught across Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana schools; some Theravada teachers follow the sixteen steps of the Anapanasati Sutta, beginning with simply knowing long and short breaths.
